title: Research Bite #19: The Curse of Knowledge When Predicting Others' Knowledge
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #19 covers Tullis and Feder's study on the "curse of knowledge" -- the tendency for people to overestimate what others know based on what they themselves know. Across four experiments, the researchers tracked both calibration (how accurate estimates are overall) and resolution (how well someone can tell easy questions from hard ones) as participants' own knowledge increased, and found that gaining expertise degraded both. The effect was strongest when participants answered a question themselves before estimating how many other people would know it, suggesting their own successful recall was contaminating the judgment. Importantly, the authors trace the bias not to over-reliance on personal experience but to a lack of any better cue about what others actually know -- when you strip away your own experience as a guide, you're not left with a more accurate substitute, just more noise. For teachers, who must constantly judge what students already understand in order to plan and pace lessons, this is a direct warning: subject-matter expertise itself works against accurate estimation of a class's knowledge, making formative assessment and student-facing data more important than instructor intuition.
points: The core finding that increased personal knowledge degrades both calibration and resolution reframes teacher expertise as a liability, not an asset, when estimating what students already know.
The bias is worst specifically when a teacher has just answered the same question themselves before judging students' likely knowledge, implicating their own correct recall as the contaminating cue.

Removing reliance on one's own knowledge doesn't fix the problem, because teachers still lack valid substitute cues about what novices actually know -- the fix has to come from external data, not just self-awareness.
The paper's suggestion that formative assessment, rather than instructor intuition, is what should drive judgments about student readiness and pacing.
quotes: This research article investigates the “curse of knowledge,” the tendency for individuals to overestimate others’ knowledge based on their own understanding.
Results showed that increased knowledge impaired both calibration and resolution, particularly when participants answered questions before estimating others’ knowledge.
The study suggests that this inaccuracy stems not from over-reliance on personal experience, but rather from a lack of sufficient cues about others’ knowledge.

As teachers gain more knowledge of a subject, they may become less accurate at judging what their students know. This is because their personal experiences become less reflective of novices’ knowledge.
Reducing reliance on their own knowledge does not improve the accuracy of the judgments of others’ knowledge because they may not have diagnostic cues about others to replace their own cues.

Inaccuracies in judgments about others and the “curse of knowledge” may result from a lack of valid cues about others, rather than tying estimates too strongly to one’s own experiences or misinterpreting fluency with answers
